resources.headline: HubSpot's 2026 Report on Best Marketing Channels for B2B and B2C
resources.fullText: Marketing in 2026 isn’t just about being everywhere: It’s about being strategic. Choosing the right marketing channels — and how to engage in each one — is one of the biggest choices you’ll make as a marketer. In 2026, most brands use five to eight channels to connect with customers, with top marketing channels including websites, email marketing, and social media. The right channel mix can vary based on your specific company, product, and target market. But it helps to benchmark yourself against others in your space to learn what’s working and what’s not. That’s why we interviewed 1,500+ marketers from around the world in HubSpot’s State of Marketing 2026 report. Read on to discover which channels are most popular and impactful for B2B and B2C companies, the top social media platforms, and how to experiment with new channels. Table of Contents Top B2B Marketing Channels Top B2C Marketing Channels Social Media Marketing Video Marketing SEO/AEO How to Find the Right Mix of Marketing Channels Embrace the Marketing Loop Top B2B Marketing Channels B2B marketing requires a different approach than consumer marketing. Brands need to prove that they understand complex business needs and engage multiple decision-makers throughout sales cycles that can last months. When we surveyed B2B marketers about their top channels, these three rose to the top as the most popular: Website/blog/SEO (used by 48.4% of B2B marketers) Email marketing (39.3%) Organic social media content (38.6%) When it comes to which channels work the best, websites and email marketing still rank at the top. In third place, however, paid social dethrones organic social media. Top three channels by ROI, as reported by marketers: Website/blog/SEO (30.2%) Email marketing (23.6%) Paid social media content (23.3%) Organic social media, content marketing, and physical events and trade shows also rank highly for B2B marketers. Interestingly, social media shopping tools are driving results in B2B — 21.9% say that social shopping is a top-performing channel. In 2026, B2B brands say they’ll increase spend in websites/blog/SEO, AI chatbots, paid social, content marketing, and video. The State of Marketing in 2026 HubSpot's Annual Marketing Trends Report AI in Marketing Branding and Growth Human-Led Creativity And More! Download the Free Report Top B2C Marketing Channels B2C brands need to capture the attention of fickle customers through engaging content that convinces people to click “buy.” Here are the top three channels B2C marketers are using in 2026: Organic social media content (used by 41.7% of B2C marketers) Website/blog/SEO (41.6%) Paid social media content (41.2%) Channels like search/display ads, physical events, influencer marketing, and mobile messaging remain popular. As for impact, social media is king. B2C marketers reported that the channels driving the top ROI are: Paid social media content (28.5%) Organic social media content (23.9%) Social media shopping tools ( 23.9%) The data shows that social shopping is more than a buzzy trend — it became one of the most impactful channels in 2025 and shows no signs of stopping in 2026. B2C brands also cite success in website/blog/SEO marketing, email marketing, and brand awareness efforts. In 2026, consumer brands plan to increase investments in content marketing, organic social media content, and influencer marketing. Social Media Marketing This year’s HubSpot State of Marketing shows that social media marketing is driving real results for brands: more than email marketing, display ads, events, or any kind of physical advertising. According to HubSpot’s State of Marketing Report, Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube remain the dominant trio, each used by roughly 70% of brands. Instagram leads in ROI, with 47.4% of B2C marketers ranking it a top performer, thanks to its powerful blend of visual storytelling, Reels, and shoppable features. TikTok continues its rapid ascent: 57% of brands now use it compared with 33.9% in 2025, and 35% cite high ROI. Top 5 Social Media Channels by Usage Instagram (70%) Facebook (69.6%) YouTube (68.6%) TikTok (56.5%) X (Twitter) (55.8%) LinkedIn remains popular with B2B, used by 47% of companies, but video platforms like YouTube and TikTok have surpassed it in both popularity and ROI. Brands engaging on Reddit grew substantially this year, from 11.3% in 2025 to 15.4% in 2026. Notably, investment is shifting: B2C teams are pouring budget into TikTok, Instagram, and social commerce tools, while B2B marketers are deepening their focus on LinkedIn and video. Pro Tips for Social Media Marketing in 2026 Want to know how to succeed in 2026? Platform-native content wins. Different people use different platforms for different purposes. Your 25-year-old customer who’s scrolling Instagram late at night probably wants to be entertained, not have an intellectual discussion (save that for X or LinkedIn!). Marketers who tailor creative to each channel’s format and audience outperform those who simply cross-post. Segment your audience and create unique, channel-specific content to perform on each. “It might be the same product, and it might be the same solution. But in the end, you’re focused on that audience in a way that allows the content to resonate,” says Susan Ganeshan, CMO of Emplifi. Video Marketing If you’ve yet to invest in video marketing, make 2026 your year. According to HubSpot’s State of Marketing Report, short-form video now delivers the highest ROI of any media format, with 48.6% of marketers ranking it in their top three for performance. Across industries and markets, I’ve found that video can be a great way to boost conversions, improve ROI, reach new audiences, and help you build relationships with current customers. Short-form video — under 60 seconds, optimized for sound-off, vertical viewing — dominates, especially on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts. And it’s not just for B2C: 44% of B2B brands now use it for content like product demos, c
keyNotes: Even for businesses selling to other businesses (B2B), social media shopping tools are surprisingly effective, with 21.9% of marketers saying they are a top performer, which shows that even serious business buyers are using these features.

While social media gets a lot of buzz, for businesses selling to other businesses (B2B), traditional methods like websites and email marketing still deliver the best financial returns, with websites bringing in 30.2% and email marketing 23.6% of the top results.

Although LinkedIn is still a popular social media platform for B2B companies (used by 47%), video platforms like YouTube and TikTok are now more popular and actually provide better results for businesses trying to reach other businesses.

Short videos, the kind you see on platforms like TikTok or Instagram, are not just for consumer brands; 44% of businesses selling to other businesses (B2B) are now using them for things like product demonstrations, and they deliver the highest return on investment (ROI) of any media format.

Simply posting the same message everywhere doesn't work; successful marketers create different versions of their content for each social media platform and its specific audience, like using entertaining videos for Instagram and more serious discussions for LinkedIn.
resources.question: The article emphasizes that effective marketing means being strategic and tailoring your message to each platform and audience, rather than just being everywhere. If you had to explain a complex idea from your own job to three very different groups – for example, a new intern, a senior executive, and a potential new customer – how would you change your explanation for each, and what 'channels' (like a quick chat, an email, or a detailed presentation) would you choose to deliver it?

resources.headline: Pardot alternatives: What B2B marketers are choosing now
resources.fullText: Seventy percent of marketers believe the marketing industry has changed more in the past three years than in the past 50. That means that marketing automation platforms need to change, too. Pardot is a longtime fixture of the B2B landscape, but the lack of development has left many businesses looking for alternatives. Why are businesses leaving? What Pardot alternatives are they choosing, and what do experts say about having a successful migration? This guide answers all these questions and more. Why Marketers Are Seeking Pardot Alternatives Now Pardot (rebranded as Marketing Cloud Account Engagement in 2022) is a B2B marketing automation platform owned by Salesforce. According to Pardot expert Tom Ryan, founder of MarCloud, many Pardot users choose to leave because they fear it will be discontinued. Ryan has been a Pardot consultant since 2016 and feels the eventual discontinuation is obvious. “There’s no development on the platform,” he explains. “There’s a clear migration path.” To Ryan, it feels like “it’s just a case of ‘when’ not ‘if.‘” Beyond discontinuation fears, Ryan points to revenue attribution and reporting as persistent pain points. Revenue attribution is “[incredibly difficult] if you do not know how to do it. Users need to wrestle with the Pardot-Salesforce sync,” he said. Reporting presents similar challenges, as the platform offers little flexibility. “The reports are not customizable in Pardot and therefore, people cannot get the reports they need. Clear reporting in general is very difficult for people to achieve, without consultant-level knowledge.” In Ryan’s experience, the most common destination for customers leaving Pardot is HubSpot. “Pardot to HubSpot makes the most sense. There’s a lot of architectural similarities between Pardot and HubSpot via the connector. So there’s a familiarity there, and you get so much more.” Free Marketing Software Easy marketing tools that deliver fast time-to-value, unified in one place. AI Tools Email Marketing Social Media Management And More! Get free marketing software How to Evaluate Pardot Alternatives for B2B Teams Pardot alternatives should be evaluated on CRM integration. HubSpot and Zoho both offer full CRM capabilities, making them top candidates for businesses leaving Salesforce altogether. Salesforce Marketing Cloud Next runs natively on Salesforce’s own platform, so there’s no separate system to sync at all, eliminating the data silo issue that Pardot has. Marketo maintains a native two-way Salesforce sync for teams that want to keep their CRM there. ActiveCampaign offers the same native Salesforce sync, plus its own lightweight CRM for teams that want to consolidate instead. B2B teams should also weigh these criteria when reviewing Pardot alternatives. ABM and lead scoring: Does the platform support both individual lead scoring and coordinated outreach across a group? Sales alignment: Is the data easy for sales to access? Integrations: Does the new platform integrate with your existing marketing tech stack: email marketing, analytics, reporting tools, etc.? Time-to-value: Can a marketer build and launch without a developer or certified consultant, or does every task require outside help? HubSpot Marketing Automation HubSpot Marketing Automation builds multi-step B2B nurture workflows that trigger based on behavior, lifecycle stage, or CRM data. The tool is designed for marketers who want their data under one roof with HubSpot’s Smart CRM, alleviating the pain points of Pardot’s siloed design and clunky features. Teams can replace Salesforce CRM with HubSpot CRM, or use the native two-way sync to keep contacts, companies, deals, and activity history aligned across both platforms. Key HubSpot Features Marketing automation: Build multi-step nurture workflows that trigger based on a prospect’s behavior, lifecycle stage, or CRM data. This replaces the rigid workflows in Pardot with something marketers can build and adjust themselves. Marketing campaigns: Connect social, ads, emails, and landing pages into one tracked campaign. This allows B2B teams to measure cross-channel impact without manually piecing data together between sources. Source Lead scoring: Ranks prospects by fit and engagement so sales teams receive only qualified leads. Contact management: Unifies sales and marketing data on a single contact record so handoffs between teams don’t require syncing across separate platforms. Website tracking: Track organic search traffic and site visitor behavior with HubSpot’s built-in analytics, plus a native Google Analytics 4 integration. Advanced marketing reporting: Attribute revenue back to specific channels and campaigns so B2B marketers can validate ROI to leadership. keyNotes: A surprising 70% of marketers feel their industry has changed more in the last three years than in the previous fifty, which means the software they use to automate marketing tasks also needs to evolve quickly.

One long-standing marketing tool, Pardot, is causing concern among its users because an expert believes it shows 'no development' and will eventually be discontinued, making businesses look for new options.

Many users struggle with Pardot because it's incredibly difficult to figure out which marketing efforts actually lead to sales (called 'revenue attribution') and its reports are not customizable, meaning they can't easily get the data they need.

When businesses leave Pardot, many choose HubSpot because it has a similar structure, making the switch easier, and it offers more features, like bringing all your customer data together in one place.

When picking a new marketing tool, it's crucial to check how well it connects with your customer information system (called 'CRM integration') and if it allows marketers to build and launch campaigns without needing a developer or consultant, which is known as 'time-to-value'.
resources.question: The article mentions that some marketing tools require 'consultant-level knowledge' or outside help for every task, impacting how quickly a team can get value from the software. In your own work, how often do you find yourself needing specialized external help for tasks that you feel should be straightforward, and what impact does that have on your team's ability to move forward quickly?

resources.headline: YouTube Measures Creator Video on Branded Search Lift, But The Attribution Gap Still Exists via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: Google is now promoting YouTube creator partnerships on branded search outcomes, as well as on views, engagement, and subscribers, but the playbook making that pitch never explains how a brand without an internal data science team is supposed to measure it. Buried inside “Creator Marketing: Build Edition,” the case studies are doing something more specific than proving creator content works. They’re proving it moves the same metric SEOs have spent two decades optimizing for directly: branded search demand. Three of the four headline case studies lead with the reach and engagement metrics YouTube has sold against for more than 15 years. Adobe’s page leads with Kinigra Deon’s 5.9 million subscribers, a scale metric, not a lift metric. The L’Oréal case study leads with an 82% surge in overall views per mention, an engagement number. Coach’s success story leads with a 60% increase in awareness among Gen Z, a survey metric. Supergoop Is The One That Leads With Search Supergoop’s case study is the exception. The brand’s headline numbers, a 93% increase in searches for hero product Glowscreen and a 55% increase in searches for the Supergoop brand name itself, are the only figures in this document stated directly in branded search terms rather than views, subscribers, or survey-based awareness. Google building a creator case study around demand behavior it can trace back to a search bar instead of a watch counter is a positioning move worth taking seriously even though it’s currently a sample size of one inside Google’s own playbook. L’Oréal’s Executives Are Making An SEO Argument With A Views Number The L’Oréal case study is also worth pulling apart. Ariana Parasco, the brand’s SVP of Brand and Consumer Engagement, describes L’Oréal’s creator-roster strategy as building “an always-on discovery infrastructure that appreciates in value over time.” The metric attached to that quote is a views number, not a search number, so the language and the data are running ahead of each other. What Parasco is describing, an asset that keeps generating discovery value long after the campaign budget stops spending, is a classic SEO argument about compounding content value. That gap between the language brand executives are reaching for and the metric Google chose to report is itself worth noting, separate from whatever Supergoop proved. Google hasn’t repositioned creator marketing around search outcomes across the board, and the playbook’s other three flagship case studies prove that. What Google has done here is publish one case study willing to lead with branded search lift as its headline metric instead of defaulting to subscribers, engagements, or views, and that’s a template other advertisers and other case studies will likely follow before long. Supergoop got there first. The rest of the playbook hasn’t caught up, and neither has the measurement guidance. What Supergoop’s Page Doesn’t Tell You That guidance gap represents a strategic opportunity. Even isolated to the one case study that reports it, Supergoop’s search lift numbers arrive with no disclosed attribution window, no baseline period, and no explanation of how the brand isolated the creator campaign’s effect on branded search from whatever paid media or seasonal demand for sunscreen was running the same month. A 93% increase is meaningless without knowing what it’s a percentage of, over what window, against what control. If Supergoop’s page is the template Google wants other advertisers to chase, the methodology behind it needs to be published alongside the result, not implied by it. How To Build The Case Your CMO Wants So, here’s how to build your own version of the Supergoop case, assuming that’s the story your CMO actually wants and not a subscriber count. Set your branded search baseline before the creator content goes live. Pull branded query impressions and click-through rate from Search Console, or a branded-term index from a tool like Glimpse or Google Trends, for a defined pre-campaign window, ideally four to six weeks, so the lift you report is measured against a real number rather than reconstructed after the fact. Separate search volume from search capture. A rise in branded search demand that isn’t matched by a rise in your own organic click-through rate for those same brand terms means an AI Overview, a competitor’s bid, or the creator’s own video is intercepting that demand before it reaches your site. Track both numbers side by side rather than reporting volume alone. Run a holdout, not a before-and-after comparison. Hold a geography or an audience segment out of the creator flight and compare branded search behavior against the markets that saw it. That’s the only way to credit the creator campaign specifically, rather than whatever paid media or PR was running the same week, and it’s the step missing from every case study in this playbook, Supergoop included. Google proved a creator campaign can move branded search demand and be willing to say so in public. It didn’t prove that’s how creator marketing gets measured now, and until three more case studies look like Supergoop’s, I’d treat that page as a proof of concept to replicate carefully, not a new industry default. More Resources: The AI Overviews YouTube Gap: The Platform Your Team Skipped For 20 Years AI Video After Sora: 3 Updates You Should Make Before You Publish YouTube’s AI Slop Problem And How Marketers Can Compete Featured Image: Roman Samborskyi/Shutterstock Category Video Advertising YouTube
keyNotes: Even though YouTube is trying to show that videos made by creators can make more people search for a company's name or product (called "branded search"), they don't clearly explain how companies can actually measure if this is happening.

Most of YouTube's examples of successful creator campaigns still focus on old ways of measuring success, like how many people watched a video or how many followers a creator has, instead of directly showing if more people are looking for the brand.

Only one company, Supergoop, showed a clear increase in "branded search" for its products (a 93% increase for Glowscreen and 55% for the brand name), but even their example didn't explain *how* they knew the video caused this increase, making it hard to fully trust the numbers.

To truly know if a creator video works, companies should measure how many people search for their brand *before* the video, and also compare results in areas where the video was shown versus areas where it wasn't, instead of just looking at numbers after the fact.
resources.question: The article highlights how difficult it is to truly prove that a specific marketing effort, like a video from a creator, directly causes more people to search for a company's product. In your own field, where do you find it most challenging to connect a specific action you take to a clear, measurable result, and what methods do you use to try and bridge that "measurement gap"?

keyNotes: The article warns that old, forgotten information you have online can actually hurt your brand, especially because new AI search tools might find and use it in ways you don't expect. This means you need to actively manage all your online content, not just the new stuff.

Many companies face something called "content debt," which is like having a lot of old, messy, or unhelpful information that needs to be fixed or removed. This problem can make it hard to create good new content or use new technologies effectively.

New technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) are dramatically changing how marketing teams work and what skills they need. The article suggests AI is "blowing up" old ways of doing things and reshaping job roles, making it crucial to adapt.

To handle all this content and new technology, businesses need a clear system for managing their online information, often called "content operations" or "orchestration." This helps avoid "content chaos" and ensures everything works together smoothly.
resources.question: The article highlights how 'outdated content' can become a 'liability' with new AI search tools. Thinking about the information your organization puts out, what kind of 'old' or 'forgotten' content might unknowingly be shaping how people perceive your brand today?

Even with all the new ways to reach people, email is still a very powerful tool for businesses, delivering the best return on investment (meaning, for every dollar you spend, you get the most back).

keyNotes: Sometimes, just looking at numbers isn't enough; the article titles suggest that direct conversations can reveal important insights that data alone cannot, as highlighted in "What Data Can't Tell You (But a Conversation Can)."

It's easy to get caught up in "vanity metrics," which are numbers that might look impressive but don't actually show real business impact; a good measurement plan goes beyond these, according to "5-Step Content Measurement Framework That Goes Beyond Vanity Metrics."

Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a major factor in how companies measure and understand their marketing efforts, with several article titles focusing on "Measuring Content Marketing in the AI Age."

Understanding the true "ROI" (Return on Investment), which means how much profit or benefit a company gets from its marketing spending, is a frequent challenge, and there are new ways top leaders should measure this, as discussed in "The New Rules of Content ROI."

Simply presenting charts and graphs isn't always effective; the article titles suggest that turning data into compelling "stories" is crucial for gaining support from important people within an organization, as seen in "Why Stories, Not Charts, Hold the Power in Data-Driven Decisions."
